title: Humanitarian Intervention, Responsibility to Protect, and the Limits of Sovereignty
seo_title: Humanitarian Intervention and Responsibility to Protect
previous_article: Self-Defense, Collective Security, and the UN Charter Framework
next_article: International Humanitarian Law: The Geneva Conventions and the Regulation of Armed Conflict
excerpt_139_words: Humanitarian intervention and the responsibility to protect sit at the boundary between sovereignty, non-intervention, and the protection of populations from mass atrocity. This article explains how international law treats claims that force may be used to prevent genocide, war crimes, ethnic cleansing, and crimes against humanity, while preserving the Charter prohibition on unilateral force. It examines Article 2(4), Security Council authorization, R2P’s three-pillar framework, the 2005 World Summit Outcome, Libya, Kosovo, Rwanda, Srebrenica, Syria, Palestine and Gaza, Global South critique, mandate discipline, and the risk that humanitarian language can become a pretext for regime change or geopolitical intervention. By connecting doctrine, institutions, case law, and lawyer-facing workflows, the article shows why civilian protection is legally urgent but cannot be separated from consent, collective security, and the limits of sovereignty.
